masteryZone.q: Which of the following acts was the first step taken by the British Parliament to control and regulate the affairs of the East India Company in India?
opts: Pitt's India Act of 1784
Regulating Act of 1773
Charter Act of 1793
Amending Act of 1781
masteryZone.sol: The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first step by the British Parliament to control and regulate the affairs of the EIC in India.

masteryZone.q: Who was appointed as the first Governor-General of Bengal under the Regulating Act of 1773?
opts: Lord Cornwallis
Robert Clive
Warren Hastings
William Bentinck
masteryZone.sol: Warren Hastings was appointed the first Governor-General of Bengal, assisted by an Executive Council of four members.

masteryZone.q: Which act established the Board of Control to manage political affairs, creating a system of Double Government?
opts: Regulating Act of 1773
Amending Act of 1781
Pitt's India Act of 1784
Charter Act of 1813
masteryZone.sol: Pitt's India Act of 1784 created the Board of Control for political affairs while the Court of Directors managed commercial affairs, starting the Double Government.

masteryZone.q: Lord Cornwallis was appointed as the Governor-General of Bengal and Commander-in-Chief. Which legislative act granted him overriding powers over his council?
opts: Regulating Act of 1773
Act of 1786
Charter Act of 1793
Pitt's India Act of 1784
masteryZone.sol: The Act of 1786 was passed to meet Lord Cornwallis's conditions, granting him Commander-in-Chief powers and overriding power over his council.

masteryZone.q: The Supreme Court of Judicature established at Calcutta in 1774 consisted of a Chief Justice and how many other judges?
opts: Two other judges
Three other judges
Four other judges
Five other judges
masteryZone.sol: The Supreme Court established in 1774 at Calcutta under the 1773 Act consisted of one Chief Justice (Sir Elijah Impey) and three other judges.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following were provisions of the Regulating Act of 1773? (Select all that apply)
opts: It made the Governors of Bombay and Madras Presidencies subordinate to the Governor-General of Bengal.
It prohibited the servants of the EIC from engaging in private trade.
It established a Board of Control consisting of six Commissioners.
It prohibited the EIC servants from accepting presents or bribes from natives.
masteryZone.sol: The 1773 Act subordinated Bombay and Madras governors, prohibited private trade, and banned bribes. The Board of Control was established in 1784, not 1773.

masteryZone.q: Identify the features of the Amending Act of 1781 (Act of Settlement) from the following: (Select all that apply)
opts: It exempted the Governor-General and his Council from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction for official acts.
It excluded revenue matters from the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
It directed the Supreme Court to administer personal laws of the native defendants.
It created a new body called the Board of Control to manage political affairs.
masteryZone.sol: The 1781 Act exempted the GG, his council, and revenue matters from SC jurisdiction, and protected personal laws. The Board of Control was created in 1784.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following changes were introduced by Pitt's India Act of 1784? (Select all that apply)
opts: It designated EIC's territories in India as 'British possessions'.
It gave the British Government supreme control over EIC affairs and administration in India.
It reduced the number of members in the Governor-General's Executive Council from 4 to 3.
It abolished the Court of Directors.
masteryZone.sol: Pitt's India Act designated territories as 'British possessions', gave the Crown supreme control, and reduced GG council members from 4 to 3. It did not abolish the Court of Directors (which happened in 1858).

masteryZone.q: What were the primary demands of Lord Cornwallis before accepting the office of Governor-General? (Select all that apply)
opts: He should be given overriding power over his executive council in special cases.
He should also be made the Commander-in-Chief of the forces.
The trade monopoly of the EIC should be completely abolished immediately.
The Board of Control should be headed by an Indian representative.
masteryZone.sol: Lord Cornwallis demanded overriding powers in special cases and the post of Commander-in-Chief, both of which were granted by the Act of 1786.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following statements about the Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774) are correct? (Select all that apply)
opts: Sir Elijah Impey was its first Chief Justice.
It was established under the provisions of the Regulating Act of 1773.
It had jurisdiction over all British subjects in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
Its judges were appointed directly by the Court of Directors.
masteryZone.sol: Sir Elijah Impey was the first CJ, it was created under the 1773 Act, and had jurisdiction over British subjects in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. The judges were appointed by the Crown, not EIC Directors.

masteryZone.q: The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first time the British Parliament recognized the political functions of the East India Company.
masteryZone.sol: True. The Act recognized for the first time the political and administrative functions of the Company.

masteryZone.q: The Governor-General of Bengal was given absolute veto power over his Executive Council by the Regulating Act of 1773.
masteryZone.sol: False. Warren Hastings did not have veto power in 1773; decisions were by majority vote and he only had a casting vote in case of ties.

masteryZone.q: The Amending Act of 1781 is also known as the Act of Settlement.
masteryZone.sol: True. The Amending Act of 1781 was enacted to settle jurisdictional conflicts and is known as the Act of Settlement.

masteryZone.q: Under the Act of Settlement 1781, provincial courts' appeals were to be taken to the Supreme Court of Calcutta.
masteryZone.sol: False. Appeals from provincial courts were to be taken to the Governor-General-in-Council, not the Supreme Court.

masteryZone.q: Pitt's India Act of 1784 established a system of Double Government.
masteryZone.sol: True. It created a system of Double Government with the Board of Control (political) and Court of Directors (commercial).

masteryZone.q: The Board of Control established in 1784 was headed by EIC Shareholders.
masteryZone.sol: False. The Board of Control was a Crown body consisting of British cabinet ministers and Commissioners, not EIC shareholders.

masteryZone.q: The Act of 1786 was passed specifically to satisfy the demands of Lord Cornwallis.
masteryZone.sol: True. It granted Cornwallis overriding powers and the Commander-in-Chief title before he accepted the Governor-Generalship.

masteryZone.q: Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of India.
masteryZone.sol: False. Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal (1773). Lord William Bentinck was the first Governor-General of India (1833).

masteryZone.q: Why did the British Parliament pass the Regulating Act of 1773?
masteryZone.sol: The EIC was facing a severe financial crisis and requested a loan from the British Government. Additionally, EIC servants were accumulating massive personal fortunes through corruption and private trade, which prompted parliamentary intervention to regulate and control EIC affairs.

masteryZone.q: Why was the Amending Act of 1781 (Act of Settlement) enacted?
masteryZone.sol: The Regulating Act of 1773 had not defined the jurisdiction boundaries between the newly created Supreme Court and the Governor-General-in-Council. This led to serious clashes, such as Supreme Court warrants against EIC revenue collectors. The 1781 Act was passed to resolve these executive-judicial conflicts by exempting official acts and revenue matters from SC jurisdiction.

masteryZone.q: Why was the system of Double Government established under Pitt's India Act of 1784?
masteryZone.sol: The British Government wanted to assert political control over EIC's growing territories without directly taking over its commercial trade operations. Hence, they separated the commercial functions (under Court of Directors) and political administration (under Crown-controlled Board of Control).

masteryZone.q: How did the Regulating Act of 1773 change the administrative structure of the Presidencies in India?
masteryZone.sol: Before 1773, the Presidencies of Bengal, Bombay, and Madras were independent of each other. The 1773 Act changed this by making the Governors of Bombay and Madras subordinate to the Governor-General of Bengal, initiating the process of administrative centralization in India.

masteryZone.q: How did the Amending Act of 1781 protect the personal laws of native Indians in judicial proceedings?
masteryZone.sol: The 1781 Act directed the Supreme Court of Calcutta to respect and administer the personal laws of the native defendants in all cases. It mandated that Hindu defendants be tried according to Hindu laws and Muslim defendants according to Islamic laws, preventing the forced application of English common law on native traditions.

masteryZone.q: How did Pitt's India Act 1784 resolve the problem of decision deadlocks in the Governor-General's Council?
masteryZone.sol: The 1773 Act had created a 4-member council where the Governor-General needed at least 2 members to support him to pass a decision. Pitt's India Act reduced the council strength to 3. This allowed the Governor-General (who had a casting vote in case of ties) to pass decisions with the support of just one council member, easing the executive deadlock.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: The Trial of Raja Nandakumar (1775). Analyze the conflict between the Executive and Judiciary under the 1773 Act.
masteryZone.sol: In 1775, Raja Nandakumar accused Governor-General Warren Hastings of corruption. Shortly after, Nandakumar was arrested for forgery, tried by the Supreme Court (headed by Hastings' friend Impey), and sentenced to death under English law. This case highlighted the severe constitutional flaw of the 1773 Act: the lack of clear boundaries between the Executive and Supreme Court, which allowed the court to be weaponized for political purposes. This crisis directly led to the Amending Act of 1781.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: The Creation of Double Government (1784). Evaluate the political impact of this system on EIC's autonomy.
masteryZone.sol: Pitt's India Act 1784 split EIC's operations. The Board of Control (Crown body) got complete veto power over political despatches, military movements, and revenues. While the Court of Directors retained commercial patronage, the company lost its political sovereignty. This system allowed the British Cabinet to control Indian foreign policy and imperial expansion while leaving trade operations to EIC, making EIC a subordinate political agent of the Crown.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: The Governor-General's Veto Power and Council (1786). Assess the constitutional significance of the Act of 1786.
masteryZone.sol: Cornwallis refused to take office as Governor-General unless he was given the authority to override his council in special cases and was made the Commander-in-Chief. The Act of 1786 met these demands. This set a precedent where future Governor-Generals were vested with concentrated civil and military powers, transforming the Governor-Generalship from a consensual chair of a council into a powerful local autocrat.

masteryZone.q: Teach the Concept: The difference between Court of Directors and Board of Control.
masteryZone.sol: Explain that the Court of Directors was the corporate body representing the shareholders of the East India Company, managing trade, commercial operations, and hiring company staff. The Board of Control was a British government body consisting of six Privy Councillors (led by a Cabinet minister) appointed by the Crown to supervise and direct all political, civil, and military affairs in India.

masteryZone.q: Teach the Concept: Centralization vs. Decentralization under EIC Rule.
masteryZone.sol: Use a conceptual timeline to explain that centralization began in 1773 when Bombay and Madras governors were subordinated to Bengal. Pitt's India Act in 1784 furthered this by giving supreme authority to London. Explain that centralization was driven by the need to present a unified military front against Indian powers, though it severely weakened regional administration.

masteryZone.q: Teach the Concept: The casting vote of the Governor-General under the Regulating Act 1773.
masteryZone.sol: Explain that decisions in the GG's council of 4 members were taken by majority vote. If the council members voted 2 vs 2, the Governor-General could use a second vote (the casting vote) to break the tie and pass the bill. However, if his council voted 3 vs 1 against him, his casting vote was useless, making him subordinate to his council.

The collapse of EIC's trade revenues due to corruption.
masteryZone.sol: British merchants lobbied for trade access due to blockades in Europe by Napoleon's continental system, forcing parliament to end EIC's monopoly in 1813.

masteryZone.q: The Charter Act of 1793 abolished the EIC trade monopoly in India.

masteryZone.q: The payment of Board of Control salaries out of Indian revenues was introduced by the Charter Act of 1793.

masteryZone.q: Under the 1793 Act, any senior official leaving India without permission was considered to have resigned.

masteryZone.q: Napoleon's Continental System had no influence on the passing of the Charter Act of 1813.
masteryZone.sol: False. The Continental System closed European markets to British goods, forcing the British government to open Indian trade to private merchants.

masteryZone.sol: False. The 1813 Act permitted missionaries to enter India under licenses.

masteryZone.q: Why was the Charter Act of 1793 significant for EIC finances?
masteryZone.sol: It extended the trade monopoly for 20 years, ensuring EIC commercial profits. However, it also introduced a major financial burden: charging the salaries of the Board of Control and its staff to EIC's Indian revenues, initiating the official drain of wealth.

masteryZone.q: Why did the British Parliament choose to retain the tea and China trade monopolies for EIC in 1813?
masteryZone.sol: The tea trade with China was highly lucrative and required complex diplomatic networks. The British parliament feared that opening the tea and China trade to unregulated private merchants would disrupt trade relations with the Qing Dynasty and cause EIC financial collapse, so they retained these monopolies as a compromise.

masteryZone.q: Why did the Anglicist-Orientalist controversy delay the execution of the 1813 education grant?
masteryZone.sol: The Rs 1 Lakh education grant did not specify whether the medium of instruction should be English (Anglicist view) or native languages (Orientalist view), and whether the content should be Western sciences or traditional Indian literature. This ideological divide prevented any funds from being utilized until Macaulay's Minute in 1835.

masteryZone.q: How did the Continental System of Napoleon indirectly affect EIC's trade monopoly in India?
masteryZone.sol: Napoleon's Continental System closed European ports to British trade. This caused severe losses to British manufacturers and merchants, who pressured the British Parliament to open the Indian market for private trade, leading to the abolition of EIC's trade monopoly under the Charter Act of 1813.

masteryZone.q: How did the Charter Act of 1793 affect senior officials who wished to travel to Britain?
masteryZone.sol: The 1793 Act introduced a strict rule: if any Governor-General, Governor, Commander-in-Chief, or senior administrator left India to return to Europe, it was legally treated as a resignation from service. They could not resume office without a new appointment, preventing them from leaving their posts without permission.

masteryZone.q: How did the Charter Act of 1813 alter the constitutional status of the East India Company?
masteryZone.sol: The 1813 Act altered the EIC status by formally asserting the sovereignty of the British Crown over Indian territories. This turned EIC from a politically independent commercial body into a political trustee holding territories on behalf of the British Crown, laying the ground for eventual Crown takeover.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: The Pressure of Manchester Lobby (1813). Evaluate the shift from mercantilism to free trade.
masteryZone.sol: In the early 19th century, the Industrial Revolution in Britain (centered in Manchester) created a massive textile surplus. The Manchester lobby campaigned against EIC's monopoly, arguing it restricted markets for British goods. By abolishing the monopoly in 1813, the British Parliament shifted from EIC's mercantilist model (buying Indian goods to sell in Europe) to a colonial market model (importing raw materials from India and exporting cheap manufactured goods to India), which de-industrialized native Indian handicraft industries.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: The Payment of Board of Control Salaries (1793). Analyze the financial impact on EIC's territorial revenue.
masteryZone.sol: The 1793 Act mandated that the salaries and expenses of the Board of Control (British Cabinet ministers) be paid from EIC's Indian territorial revenues. This was a critical shift: Indian taxes were being used to pay the salaries of British cabinet members in London. This precedent formalized the drain of wealth, where Indian revenues were spent directly on British administrative overheads, reducing the capital available for local development.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: The Entry of Christian Missionaries (1813). Analyze the socio-religious impact of this provision.
masteryZone.sol: The EIC had banned missionaries to avoid upsetting native religious sentiments and disrupting trade. The 1813 Act forced EIC to allow them entry. Missionaries established schools, printing presses, and hospitals. While this promoted modern education and social reform (e.g., campaign against Sati), it also created native resentment due to conversion attempts, which contributed to cultural anxieties and set the stage for subsequent religious-reform movements and conflicts.

masteryZone.q: Teach the Concept: Napoleon's Continental System and its trade implications.
masteryZone.sol: Explain that the Continental System was Napoleon's foreign policy blockade against Great Britain during the Napoleonic Wars. It banned all European nations under French control from trading with Britain, aiming to ruin British trade. Explain how this blockade caused a massive crisis in Britain, forcing merchants to demand the opening of India's trade, leading to the 1813 Act.

masteryZone.q: Teach the Concept: The concept of Crown Sovereignty over EIC territories.
masteryZone.sol: Explain that 'Sovereignty' refers to the supreme, absolute political authority of a state. In 1813, the British Parliament declared the sovereignty of the Crown over EIC's territories. This meant that while EIC ran day-to-day administration, the land legally belonged to the British State, and Parliament had the ultimate right to legislate, tax, or annex it.

masteryZone.q: Teach the Concept: The Orientalist-Anglicist education debate.
masteryZone.sol: Explain that Orientalists (like William Jones) believed that education in India should be conducted in native languages (Sanskrit, Persian) focusing on traditional literature and philosophy. Anglicists (like Macaulay) argued that education should be in English, focusing on Western science and literature, to create a class of Indians 'English in taste and opinions' to serve the colonial administration.

masteryZone.q: Why was the office of Governor-General of India created in 1833?
masteryZone.sol: The British Parliament wanted to establish complete political and administrative centralization over all EIC territories in India. By renaming the Governor-General of Bengal to Governor-General of India and vesting in him all civil, military, and exclusive legislative powers, they created a single executive head for the entire country.

masteryZone.q: Why did the Charter Act of 1853 create the Central Legislative Council?
masteryZone.sol: The administrative load of EIC had increased significantly, and the executive council was struggling to perform both governing duties and lawmaking tasks. By adding 6 new legislative councilors, the Act separated legislative and executive functions, creating a dedicated legislative body to systematically debate and pass laws.

masteryZone.q: Why is the Charter Act of 1853 considered a signal of EIC's imminent termination?
masteryZone.sol: Unlike previous charter acts (1793, 1813, 1833) which renewed the EIC charter for a fixed term of 20 years, the 1853 Act extended EIC's administration without specifying any time limit. Sourcing EIC's hold 'in trust' without a timeline clearly indicated that the British Parliament could take over direct control of India at any time.

masteryZone.q: How did the Charter Act of 1833 centralize legislative powers in India?
masteryZone.sol: The 1833 Act completely stripped the Governors of Bombay and Madras Presidencies of their legislative powers. The Governor-General of India in Council was vested with exclusive legislative authority to make laws for the entire British India, and any law passed by GGI was called an 'Act', whereas earlier presidency laws were called 'Regulations'.

masteryZone.q: How did the Charter Act of 1853 change the recruitment of civil servants in India?
masteryZone.sol: The 1853 Act abolished EIC's patronage system, under which directors nominated candidates for civil service posts. It introduced an open competitive examination system, allowing all qualified candidates, including Indians, to compete on merit, which led to the appointment of the Macaulay Committee in 1854 to implement the exam rules.

masteryZone.q: How did the First Law Commission of 1834 contribute to the Indian legal system?
masteryZone.sol: The First Law Commission, headed by Lord Macaulay, was appointed to codify all Indian laws, which were unstructured and based on varied personal laws and regulations. The Commission drafted the Indian Penal Code (IPC), which eventually became law in 1860, establishing a uniform criminal justice system for the entire country.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: The Centralization of 1833 and its Impact on Presidencies. Analyze the administrative consequences of stripping Bombay and Madras of legislative powers.
masteryZone.sol: The Charter Act of 1833 concentrated all lawmaking power in Bengal. The governors of Bombay and Madras had to submit all local legislative proposals to Calcutta. This led to severe delays and administrative inefficiency, as the central council in Calcutta lacked local knowledge of Bombay and Madras's revenue systems and social customs. This extreme centralization proved dysfunctional, forcing the British to reverse it in the Indian Councils Act of 1861 by restoring provincial legislative powers.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: The Macaulay Committee on Civil Services (1854). Evaluate the transition from patronage to meritocracy.
masteryZone.sol: The EIC directors used civil service nominations as commercial patronage. The 1853 Act ended this, and the 1854 Macaulay Committee drafted the competitive exam guidelines. The exam tested candidates in classical European history, mathematics, and science to recruit well-rounded administrators. This established a meritocratic, elite civil service (Covenanted Civil Service), which became the 'steel frame' of British rule in India, but the classical European syllabus kept it inaccessible to most native Indians initially.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: The Unspecified Charter Term of 1853. Analyze the political landscape that led to the Crown takeover in 1858.
masteryZone.sol: The British Parliament systematically reduced EIC's powers through the 1853 Act by reducing the number of EIC directors from 24 to 18 (with 6 nominated by the Crown) and leaving the charter extension unspecified. The company had lost its trade, patronage, and long-term lease. Sourcing EIC's weak position explains why, when the Revolt of 1857 broke out, the British Parliament faced no political obstacle in immediately liquidating the EIC and establishing direct Crown rule in 1858.

masteryZone.q: Teach the Concept: The concept of a Mini-Parliament under the 1853 Act.
masteryZone.sol: Explain that the Central Legislative Council created in 1853 functioned as a mini-parliament. It adopted the same parliamentary procedures as the British House of Commons, including reading bills three times, debating clauses, asking questions to the executive, and passing laws. This introduced representative legislative procedures to India for the first time.

masteryZone.q: Teach the Concept: The distinction between Regulations and Acts.
masteryZone.sol: Explain that before the Charter Act of 1833, the legislative powers were decentralized, and laws passed by Bengal, Madras, and Bombay presidencies were called 'Regulations'. After 1833, legislative power was centralized under the GGI, and all laws passed by the GGI Council were designated as 'Acts', establishing a uniform national legislative status.

masteryZone.q: Teach the Concept: The role of a Law Member in a colonial executive council.
masteryZone.sol: Explain that the Law Member was added in 1833 to provide professional legal expertise to the Governor-General's Council for drafting laws and codification. Initially, he could attend council meetings only during legislative debates and had no executive voting rights, representing a checks-and-balances separation between lawmaking and executive administration.
